query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in high‐entropy alloys is governed by the in situ formation and rapid self-healing of a dense, adherent passive oxide film that forms through surface enrichment of elements with high oxygen affinity (e.g., Cr or Al), which in turn provides both a chemical barrier to corrosive species and a mechanically robust layer that minimizes wear damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase matrix and no pre-existing protective surface oxide.
generation.intervention: Heat-treatment or high-temperature processing designed to promote surface segregation of high oxygen affinity elements, thereby initiating formation of a thin, continuous oxide layer prior to service.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) combined with reciprocating mechanical wear (e.g., tribometer tests) at moderate to elevated temperatures where oxygen is available for oxide reformation.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-healing, dense passive oxide film formed by the surface enrichment of elements like Cr or Al.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature processing promotes surface segregation of Cr/Al, which oxidize to form a continuous and mechanically robust passive film. This film acts as a barrier by limiting both ion penetration (thus reducing corrosion) and material removal under wear. Furthermore, if the film is abraded during service, the enrichment in the underlying matrix facilitates rapid reformation of the protective layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy processed under lower-temperature conditions (resulting in incomplete or heterogeneous surface oxide formation), the high-temperature processed HEA will exhibit a lower corrosion current density, higher passive film resistance, reduced wear depth, and a lower friction coefficient under simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions.
generation.baseline: An alloy with minimal or non-uniform surface enrichment that lacks a well-formed oxide film, leading to direct metal/solution attack and higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where there is sufficient oxygen for film formation at moderate to elevated temperatures; it may fail in oxygen-deficient atmospheres or at temperatures so high that the oxide scale spalls or becomes unstable.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between oxide film characteristics (e.g., thickness, adhesion, and healing kinetics) and the reduction in combined wear and corrosion rates is not yet fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA specimens: one processed at a higher temperature (to induce surface segregation and a continuous passive oxide film) and one processed at a lower temperature (baseline with non-ideal oxide formation). Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear and corrosion tests using a reciprocating tribometer in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at an elevated test temperature. Use real-time and post-test surface characterization (e.g., in situ EIS, potentiodynamic polarization, profilometry, and surface microscopy) to monitor oxide film integrity.
measurements: Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization
Charge transfer and passive film resistance from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Wear depth and wear rate via profilometry
Coefficient of friction during wear tests
In situ and post-test analysis of oxide film thickness and continuity using surface microscopy or spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature processed specimens fail to show statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar corrosion current density and passive film impedance) and exhibit comparable or greater wear depth and friction coefficients relative to the baseline specimens, or if the oxide film does not reform after mechanical damage, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
